name: From 17ms to 0.04ms: How to Design the Right SQL Index

chunks.content: A good SQL index comes from the queries your application runs, not from the table schema. Composite indexes need the right column order: equality columns first, then the column you sort or range on. EXPLAIN ANALYZE is how you verify it: a sequential scan over 1 million comments takes 17ms, and the right composite index answers in 0.04ms.

An index stores chosen columns in sorted order with entries pointing back to the full row. The default kind in major databases is the B-tree, which stays shallow even at millions of rows. A sequential scan reads all rows; an index scan descends a few levels and fetches only matches.

You don't pick indexes by staring at the schema; they come from the queries the application actually runs. Example access patterns for a comments table are: all comments by a user, all comments for an issue, and comments for an issue from one user, newest first, last month only.
chunks.metadata: Start With the Query, Not the Table

chunks.content: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query for real and prints the plan. Without an index, a Parallel Seq Scan over 1 million rows takes 17ms. Adding a single-column index on user_id turns the same query into an Index Only Scan in 0.6ms because the index alone can answer COUNT(*).

Column order is everything. For a query with issue_id equality, user_id equality, and created_at range ordered DESC, the composite index (issue_id, user_id, created_at DESC) answers the whole query in 0.039ms by jumping to the matching section and reading it already sorted. The leftmost prefix rule explains why (issue_id, user_id) works but (user_id) alone cannot serve an issue_id-only query.

A dashboard query fetching the 25 newest open issues with their latest comment used a LATERAL subquery. With the wrong index order, Postgres sorts 6,537 times and runs in 436ms. Reordering the index to (issue_id, created_at DESC) and adding (status, created_at DESC) on issues drops the query to 0.489ms because every node reads only what it returns.
chunks.metadata: The Query Our New Index Can't Serve

chunks.content: Indexes cost writes and disk space. Each composite index for 1 million comments is about 30 MB, versus 7 MB for single-column ones. Remove redundant indexes. An index only helps if the query can use it; wrapping an indexed column in a function makes Postgres ignore it.

Summary: design indexes from your queries, not your tables. Composite indexes need the right column order: equality columns first, then the sort or range column. LIMIT only helps when an index feeds rows already in order. EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the proof.
